meta.title: War Dogs, Part 2: The Chinese Ammo Cover-Up That Brought Them Down
meta.working_title: How the War Dogs Got Caught (War Dogs, Part 2)
meta.device: The same contract ledger from part 1, now with a red 'EVIDENCE' pile growing beside it: each email they send drops onto the pile with a thud.
meta.style: Crime-caper explainer in the house 2D style, Leo sheet style characters (same cast as part 1). Painted plates: Albanian hillside bunkers, a cardboard-box factory in Tirana, a runway in Kyrgyzstan, a Kabul airstrip, the Miami Beach office, an FBI raid, a newspaper front page, a Washington hearing room, a Miami courthouse. Khaki, rust and grey, with Miami pink fading as things go wrong. Real people stylised with no likeness. Trebicka's death described carefully: official finding stated, doubts attributed, no crash imagery. SFX under the VO (crate lids, tape guns, jet engines, door rams, gavel), music at combine.
meta.source: Same transcript as part 1 ('The Stoner Kids Dealing Guns to the Army'), second half: from the Chinese ammunition to the sentences. Based on Guy Lawson's reporting, the 2008 House Oversight Committee report and US court records. Fully rewritten.

shots.vo: Last time: two young men from Miami won a 300 million dollar Pentagon contract to arm Afghanistan. Their main source: old ammunition in Albania.
shots.visual: A quick recap: Miami flat, contract stamp, a cargo plane, Albanian bunkers.

shots.vo: Then a friend opens a crate in an Albanian bunker and sees writing he recognises. It's Chinese.
shots.visual: A crate lid lifted in torchlight; Chinese characters stencilled on the metal.

shots.vo: And selling Chinese ammunition breaks both the contract and a US ban. What they do next sends them to court.
shots.visual: A rule book with a red stamp: BANNED.
Title over the crate.

shots.vo: Neither of the bosses wants to go anywhere near Albania. So David sends his friend Alex Podrizki, a broke graduate who once served in the French army.
shots.visual: A young man with a backpack stepping off a plane in Tirana.
shots.anim: He walks out of the airport.

shots.vo: The ammunition is decades old, in rusty metal tins on rotting pallets. The workers open crates with an axe and smoke cigarettes next to gunpowder.
shots.visual: Inside a bunker: rusty tins, a worker with an axe, another smoking by a NO SMOKING sign.
shots.anim: Axe thunks; smoke curls past the sign.

shots.vo: Then he notices the writing on the tins. He calls David in Miami: you know this ammo is Chinese, right?
shots.visual: Split screen: Alex in the bunker, David in Miami, both on phones.

shots.vo: Efraim doesn't believe it. Maybe it's Korean? Send pictures. Alex emails photos. They'll later call that their first big mistake: written evidence.
shots.visual: An email with photo attachments drops onto a red EVIDENCE pile.
shots.anim: Email lands on the pile with a thud.

shots.vo: Of course it's Chinese. For decades China was Albania's only real ally, and sold it weapons. But the contract banned Chinese-made ammunition.
shots.visual: A map: an arrow from China to Albania labelled 1960s-70s.

shots.vo: They ask the State Department for an exception. The answer: only the President can approve one. No time for that. Finding other suppliers would take months.
shots.visual: A letter with 'PRESIDENTIAL DETERMINATION REQUIRED'; a calendar pages flying.

shots.vo: The safe choice was to call a lawyer and maybe lose the contract. Tens of millions of dollars were at stake. They chose to hide it.
shots.visual: A balance: 'CALL A LAWYER' on one side, '$30,000,000' on the other; the money side crashes down.

shots.vo: Merrill suggests by email removing anything that shows where the ammo came from. The plan: repack it all into plain cardboard boxes.
shots.visual: Another email drops onto the EVIDENCE pile: 'remove markings'.

shots.vo: In Tirana, Alex finds a businessman with a box factory, Kosta Trebicka. He tells him the repacking is to cut weight on the flights.
shots.visual: A cardboard factory; two men shaking hands over a stack of flat boxes.
shots.anim: Boxes fold up; tape guns zip.

shots.vo: The job: repack around 100 million rounds by hand, tin by tin, into new boxes.
shots.visual: A long line of workers moving rounds from rusty tins into brown boxes.

shots.vo: David is running shipments from all over Eastern Europe. Finally, a cargo plane with five million rounds takes off from Hungary for Kabul.
shots.visual: A cargo plane lifting off over a Hungarian airfield.

shots.vo: At a refuelling stop in Kyrgyzstan, the plane is seized. Every day on the ground costs a fortune. That's the phone call at dinner from the start of part one.
shots.visual: Guards surrounding the plane on a snowy runway; a fine meter ticking up.

shots.vo: Journalist Guy Lawson suspects Russian pressure: Moscow didn't like the US buying ammunition from other countries in its old backyard.
shots.visual: A map: a shadowy hand over Kyrgyzstan; a dollar sign pulled away.

shots.vo: Two weeks later the US defence secretary, Robert Gates, visits Kyrgyzstan. Lawson thinks freeing the plane was part of the reason. Either way, it's released.
shots.visual: An official plane landing; then the cargo plane taking off again.

shots.vo: Now about four planeloads a week land in Kabul, each with around 45 tons of munitions. Pentagon money pours into AEY's account.
shots.visual: A Kabul airstrip with planes landing in sequence; a bank meter filling.

shots.vo: Every round is stamped with where it was made. But the shipments are waved through. David and Lawson both say the Army was happy with the ammo.
shots.visual: Soldiers unloading boxes at Kabul; a clipboard stamped OK.

shots.vo: But success splits the friends. David says he's owed millions and hasn't been paid. There's no written contract. Efraim later writes he owed him nothing.
shots.visual: Two figures back to back; a torn handshake.

shots.vo: David settles for a small fraction. By then, according to Lawson, AEY had handled 85 shipments worth over 66 million dollars, with 100 million more on the way.
shots.visual: A ledger: 85 shipments, $66M; a small envelope handed to David.

shots.vo: AEY has made enemies. A rival contractor spreads a false rumour that it's selling Chinese rifles to Iraq. The Pentagon opens an investigation anyway.
shots.visual: Whispers drifting between office cubicles; a folder labelled INVESTIGATION.

shots.vo: 23 August 2007, the day David is due to sign his exit deal, federal agents raid AEY's offices and take every hard drive and file.
shots.visual: Agents in windbreakers carrying computer towers out of the Miami office.
shots.anim: Door bangs open; towers carried out.

shots.vo: On those drives: the emails. The photos of Chinese tins. The plan to repack them. The whole EVIDENCE pile, written by themselves.
shots.visual: The red EVIDENCE pile topples onto an investigator's desk.

shots.vo: David and Alex agree to cooperate with investigators.
shots.visual: Two young men across a table from agents; a pen hovering over a paper.

shots.vo: Then Kosta Trebicka, the box-factory owner, who has fallen out with the deal, passes the story to The New York Times.
shots.visual: A tip envelope sliding across a newsroom desk.

shots.vo: March 2008, it's on the front page: two young men from Miami supplying the Afghan army with old ammunition, some of it Chinese.
shots.visual: A front page spinning into frame: mugshot silhouettes next to rusty ammo tins.

shots.vo: The government is embarrassed. A congressional committee investigates, and its report is damning, mostly for the government itself.
shots.visual: A Washington hearing room; a thick report with red tabs.

shots.vo: AEY was already on a State Department watch list. Its past performance was rated unsatisfactory. It had failed earlier contracts. It still won.
shots.visual: A checklist of red flags, all ticked, then an APPROVED stamp anyway.

shots.vo: And Albania had reportedly offered to donate the ammunition for free. Then the shipments stopped, and in 2008 Afghan forces were left short.
shots.visual: A gift box labelled FREE; then an empty ammo shelf at an Afghan base.

shots.vo: In 2008 Efraim, David, Alex and Merrill are charged with fraud. Efraim, David and Alex plead guilty to conspiracy to defraud the United States. No government official is charged.
shots.visual: Four charge sheets on a desk; one marked NOT GUILTY plea.

shots.vo: David and Alex get house arrest. Stuck at home, David invents a drum-machine pedal for guitarists, and builds a business on it.
shots.visual: David at home with an ankle monitor, tinkering with a guitar pedal.
shots.anim: Pedal lights blink; he taps a beat.

shots.vo: Merrill pleads not guilty, is convicted, and gets four years. The Swiss broker Thomet is never charged, and denies any wrongdoing.
shots.visual: A gavel; a grey-suited figure walking out of frame.

shots.vo: While awaiting sentencing, Efraim is caught in an undercover sting: as a convicted felon, he picks up a gun an agent shows him. He's arrested on the spot.
shots.visual: A car boot opening; a figure reaching in; handcuffs snap.

shots.vo: In 2011 he's sentenced to four years in prison.
shots.visual: A Miami courthouse; a gavel.

acts.name: Ending: The Box-Maker and the Lesson

shots.vo: Kosta Trebicka became a witness against corruption in Albania's arms trade. In September 2008 he died when his vehicle overturned on a quiet road. Albanian officials called it an accident. Some, including Lawson, doubt that.
shots.visual: A quiet country road at dusk; a single candle; a question mark.

shots.vo: The website they used, FedBizOpps, is now called SAM.gov. The US still buys huge amounts from private contractors.
shots.visual: The old website morphing into a new one.

shots.vo: Two kids with a laptop got a 300 million dollar war contract because nobody checked properly. They were caught by their own emails. The system that hired them barely changed.
shots.visual: The ledger closes; the EVIDENCE pile; a rubber stamp still stamping.
End card.

hooks: They had a 300 million dollar Army contract. Then a friend opened a crate in Albania and saw Chinese writing.
The War Dogs weren't caught by spies or auditors. They were caught by their own emails.

fixes: NYT front page 27 March 2008 (C.J. Chivers); kept as 'March 2008'.
House Oversight Committee hearing June 2008: AEY on State Dept watch list, poor past performance. Stated as 'congressional committee'.
Indictment June 2008 (71 counts). Diveroli, Packouz, Podrizki pleaded guilty to conspiracy; Merrill convicted at trial, sentenced to 4 years.
Diveroli sentenced January 2011 to 4 years (including firearm charge).
Kyrgyzstan seizure and Russian motive are Lawson's account, attributed; Putin not named on screen or shown.
Trebicka died September 2008 in a vehicle accident; official finding accident; doubts attributed. No crash imagery.
Albania donation offer per congressional report, worded 'reportedly'.
cuts: Narrator jokes and sponsor bits removed.
